title: feet on the floor, hands on the knees
hook: feet on the floor, hands on the knees — you have one

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: the bell. Your line: arrive. Which sound became your bell? Did you arrive, even once? Day six.

Quick check. Where are your feet right now? If that took a second to answer, it's no surprise. A day can be lived about a foot above your own shoulders: in a screen, in a conversation that already happened, in tomorrow's list. Meanwhile there's a whole body down here, keeping you alive, carrying you around, sending messages that mostly go unopened. Feet on the floor. Hands on the knees. You have one. Today's three teachers, from India, from early Buddhism and from a Harvard lecture hall, all send you back to it. Today's word is body.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOUR FEET?` → `A FOOT ABOVE YOUR SHOULDERS.` → `YOU HAVE ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with an old instruction for sitting. The Yoga Sutras, compiled in India and traditionally credited to Patanjali, say almost nothing about the poses people now call yoga. On posture they are very brief. The key line is three words in Sanskrit, and it says the seat should be steady and easy. The word is asana, and in the Sutras it means simply a seat, the place you sit. Steady, so you're not fidgeting. Easy, so you're not straining. Early Buddhist texts put the body first too. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the Satipatthana Sutta, the first thing to pay attention to is the body: breathing in, breathing out, standing, walking, sitting, lying down. Knowing, plainly, what the body is doing while it's doing it. Then, in 1890, William James turned common sense around. Common sense says we cry because we're sad. James said it may run the other way. In his words, "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." Psychologists have argued about how far that goes ever since. Leave that argument to them. The smaller point is one you can check for yourself: body and feeling are tangled together, and a change in one tends to show up in the other. That's part of why the body makes such a good doorway. You can't always choose your thoughts. You can usually choose to put your feet flat on the floor. And when you do, you're somewhere definite: here, now, on the ground. A seat, a sutta, a psychologist. Not one of them needs you to believe anything first. Each just asks you to notice you're in a body.
screen: `ASANA: A SEAT, STEADY AND EASY.` · `MINDFULNESS STARTS WITH THE BODY.` · `AFRAID BECAUSE WE TREMBLE.` · `FEET FLAT ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `YOU'RE IN A BODY.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Before it rings, set your feet flat on the floor if you can, and rest your hands on your knees or in your lap. On the first breath, feel your feet. On the second, feel whatever is holding you up: the chair, the floor, the bed. On the third, feel your hands, just resting. Steady and easy. That's the whole seat.
Body. Where the mindfulness discourse starts, and a place you can always come back to. Sixth word.
Your line: come back down. Whenever you catch yourself living up in your head today, feel your feet. One breath. Come back down. Day six.

howItsDone: Yoga, Zen and many Buddhist and Christian contemplative practices begin by settling the body: a steady, comfortable seat, feet grounded, hands at rest, with attention on how the body feels.

original.note: Sanskrit, asana: a seat. Yoga Sutra 2.46 asks that it be sthira and sukha, steady and easy.

trapdoor: what you thought: the thing that carries your head around.
what it means: the place you're already sitting in, noticed on purpose.
what a scholar hears: in the Yoga Sutras asana is a seat, not a pose; the sutra gives it in three words, sthira-sukham asanam (2.46).

notes: The James-Lange view of emotion is presented as James's argument, with the caveat that psychologists still debate it; the only science claim is that body and feeling influence each other, stated modestly.
Yoga Sutras 2.46 (sthira-sukham asanam) paraphrased as 'steady and easy'; confirm with a Hindu/yoga Keeper.
Satipatthana Sutta: the body section includes breathing and the four postures; paraphrased.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener they 'probably had to think about it' or that 'most of us' live in our heads, and 'almost every contemplative path' is now just today's three sources; cut 'one of the oldest instructions', 'surprised his readers' and 'one part is widely accepted' (now 'one you can check for yourself'); asana is now what the word means in the Sutras, not an 'originally meant' etymology (speech, myth, trapdoor); replaced the repeated 'three sources, three reasons' formula; 'so many paths' cut from the word and trapdoor; match no longer says 'the quickest way back'.
